lesson.title: Series Resonance, Derived and Verified From First Principles
lesson.summary: Series resonance is the condition in a series RLC circuit where reactive impedance cancels exactly, derived here from the impedance equation and checked with a full numeric example.
lesson.body:
Series resonance formalizes everything the last several chapters have been building toward, using the tools of RLC circuit analysis and series circuits directly. Start from the impedance of a series RLC circuit as a function of frequency, Z(j omega) equals R plus j times the quantity omega L minus 1 over (omega C). The real part, R, never changes with frequency. The imaginary part, omega L minus 1 over (omega C), is negative at low frequency, where capacitive reactance dominates, positive at high frequency, where inductive reactance dominates, and crosses zero exactly once. Setting that imaginary part to zero, omega L equals 1 over (omega C), and solving for omega gives omega squared equals 1 over (LC), so the resonant angular frequency is omega_0 equals 1 over the square root of LC. At this single frequency the impedance collapses to Z equals R, purely real, current and source voltage in phase, and current at its maximum value for any given source amplitude. This is the resonance condition first introduced two chapters ago, now derived directly from the impedance equation rather than just stated.

Work through a complete numeric example from scratch. Take R equals 40 ohms, L equals 0.4 H, and C equals 0.1 microfarads, that is 1 times 10 to the negative 7 farads. First, LC equals 0.4 times (1 times 10 to the negative 7), which is 4 times 10 to the negative 8. Its square root is 2 times 10 to the negative 4, since the square root of 4 is 2 and the square root of 10 to the negative 8 is 10 to the negative 4. So omega_0 equals 1 over (2 times 10 to the negative 4), which is 5000 rad/s, or in Hz, f_0 equals 5000 over 2 pi, which is about 795.8 Hz.

Check the reactances at this frequency. X_L equals omega_0 L equals 5000 times 0.4, which is 2000 ohms. X_C equals 1 over (omega_0 C) equals 1 over (5000 times 1 times 10 to the negative 7), which is 1 over 0.0005, also 2000 ohms. They match exactly, confirming resonance, and the impedance at this frequency is Z equals R equals 40 ohms. The quality factor is Q equals X_L over R equals 2000 over 40, which is 50, a sharply selective circuit by the standard set in the previous chapter.

Now drive the circuit with a 1 V rms source at resonance. The current is I equals V over Z equals 1 over 40, which is 0.025 A, or 25 mA. The voltage across the resistor is V_R equals I times R equals 0.025 times 40, which is 1 V, matching the source exactly, since at resonance the entire source voltage appears across the resistor. The voltage across the inductor is V_L equals I times X_L equals 0.025 times 2000, which is 50 V, and the voltage across the capacitor is V_C equals I times X_C equals 0.025 times 2000, also 50 V. Both are 50 times the source voltage, matching Q equals 50 exactly.

The last step is to confirm Kirchhoff's voltage law holds, which it must for any correct circuit analysis. Taking the current as the phase reference at 0 degrees, the resistor voltage is in phase with the current, V_R equals 1 V at 0 degrees. The inductor voltage leads the current by 90 degrees, V_L equals 50 V at 90 degrees, which in rectangular form is j50. The capacitor voltage lags the current by 90 degrees, V_C equals 50 V at negative 90 degrees, which in rectangular form is negative j50. Adding all three as phasors, V_R plus V_L plus V_C equals 1 plus j50 minus j50, and the imaginary parts cancel exactly, leaving 1 V at 0 degrees, precisely the 1 V source. The two large 50 V reactive voltages are real, measurable voltages sitting across the inductor and capacitor, but they are equal, opposite, and cancel in the loop sum, which is exactly the series resonance condition, derived here from the impedance equation and verified twice over: once through the reactance values matching, and once through the full phasor sum closing back to the source voltage.
